etymology: The city in Asia Minor (modern Iznik) where the first ecumenical council met in 325; from Greek Nikaia.
biblical_def: Nicaea is the city in Asia Minor where the first ecumenical council of the church was held in the year 325, summoned to settle the great controversy raised by Arius, who taught that the Son of God was a creature, the highest of creatures, but not true and eternal God—“there was when He was not.” Against this denial of Christ’s deity the council, gathered from across the empire, confessed the Son to be “begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father”—the Greek word homoousios drawing the line that Arianism could not cross. From this council came the Nicene Creed, later expanded at Constantinople in 381 to confess fully the deity of the Holy Spirit, which remains to this day the great ecumenical confession of the Trinity, received by the church East and West. The dictionary honors Nicaea as a faithful defense of the biblical doctrine of Christ’s full and eternal deity, drawn from the Scriptures that everywhere ascribe to the Son the names, attributes, works, and worship of God. The council did not invent the doctrine but confessed what the church had always believed, against an error that struck at the heart of the gospel; for if the Son is a creature, there is no salvation, since no creature could reconcile us to God. The Reformers gladly received the Nicene faith as their own. Nicaea stands as a model of the church confessing the truth with precision when error makes precision necessary, and its creed remains a touchstone of Trinitarian orthodoxy.
webster_summary: The first ecumenical council (325), which condemned Arius and confessed the Son “of one substance with the Father,” producing the Nicene Creed—the great confession of Christ’s full deity.

corruption_summary: The Arian denial of Christ’s deity was the corruption Nicaea answered, and it has been revived in every age since.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption Nicaea answered was Arianism—the teaching of Arius that the Son is a creature, the first and highest of created beings, but not true God. Scripture forbids it: the Word was God; Christ and the Father are one; in Him dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. The council’s confession that the Son is “of one substance with the Father” drew the line precisely where the error could not cross, defending the deity on which the whole gospel depends.

The Arian error has been revived in every age—by later anti-Trinitarians, by the Socinians, by modern unitarianism, and by groups such as the Jehovah’s Witnesses, who deny the Son’s deity still. The dictionary honors Nicaea not as the invention of a doctrine but as the church’s faithful confession of what Scripture had always taught, made precise because error made precision necessary. The gospel hangs upon it: if the Son were a creature, no salvation could come through Him, for only God can reconcile men to God. The Nicene faith remains the touchstone of Trinitarian orthodoxy and the Reformers’ own confession.

etymology: The seventh ecumenical council, held at Nicaea in 787, which sanctioned the veneration of images.
biblical_def: The Second Council of Nicaea was the seventh ecumenical council, held in the year 787, which brought to an end the first iconoclastic controversy by sanctioning the veneration of images—icons of Christ, Mary, and the saints. Against the iconoclasts, who had sought to remove images from the churches as a breach of the second commandment, the council decreed that icons should be set up and given veneration and reverent honor, while distinguishing this veneration from the worship of adoration which belongs to God alone. This decision became the dogmatic foundation of the cult of icons in the Eastern Orthodox Church and undergirded the use of images in the Roman Church as well. The dictionary, holding the Reformed and biblical doctrine, judges the decree of 787 to be a sanctioning of corruption rather than a defense of orthodoxy. The second commandment expressly forbids the making of graven images and the bowing down to them in worship; the distinction between veneration and adoration, however carefully drawn, does not escape the prohibition, for Scripture forbids the religious use of images altogether and warns that the heart cannot be trusted to keep the line. The dictionary therefore stands with the iconoclasts in this matter and with the Reformation that recovered the second commandment in full, casting the images out of the churches. The Second Council of Nicaea marks the point at which image-veneration was formally established in the church, and it stands as a warning that even a great council may err when it departs from the plain word of God.

corruption_summary: The council sanctioned image-veneration, against the second commandment’s plain prohibition of the religious use of images.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the sanctioning of image-veneration itself. By decreeing that icons of Christ, Mary, and the saints should be set up and given religious veneration, the Second Council of Nicaea established in the church a practice the second commandment forbids: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image... thou shalt not bow down thyself to them.” The council’s careful distinction between veneration and adoration does not escape the prohibition, for Scripture forbids the religious use of images as such and reminds Israel that at Horeb they saw no similitude, lest they corrupt themselves with an image.

The dictionary stands with the iconoclasts in this matter and with the Reformation that recovered the second commandment in full. The LORD will not give His glory to another, neither His praise to graven images; the heart is too prone to idolatry to be trusted with the fine line the council drew, and the cult of icons that followed proved the point. The Second Council of Nicaea marks the formal establishment of image-veneration in the church, and it stands as a sober warning that even a great and ancient council may err when it departs from the plain word of God. The remedy is the worship of God in spirit and in truth, without images, as He has commanded.

etymology: From the emperor Decius, under whom it was carried out, and persecution; the empire-wide persecution of Christians in 250–251.
biblical_def: The Decian Persecution was the first systematic, empire-wide persecution of the Christian church, carried out under the Roman emperor Decius in 250 and 251. Unlike earlier local outbreaks, Decius required every inhabitant of the empire to sacrifice to the pagan gods and obtain a certificate proving they had done so. Christians who refused were imprisoned, tortured, and put to death; many of the church’s leaders, including bishops of Rome, Antioch, and Jerusalem, were martyred. The persecution was short but severe, and it tested the church profoundly. Many believers stood firm and won the martyr’s crown or endured imprisonment as confessors; but many others, unprepared for such fierce trial, fell away—some sacrificing outright, others purchasing certificates to feign compliance. These fallen ones, the lapsi, raised an agonizing question for the church after the persecution ended: on what terms might the lapsed be received back. The dictionary remembers the Decian Persecution as a great trial of faith that produced both glorious martyrs and grievous apostates, and that shaped the church’s understanding of repentance, restoration, and discipline. It stands as a witness that the world’s enmity against Christ is real and at times violent, that the Lord sustains His own in the fire while the unprepared and the false fall away, and that even the failures of the weak may, through genuine repentance, be met with the grace of God—a grace the church wrestled to administer rightly in the controversies that followed.
webster_summary: The first empire-wide persecution of the church (250–251) under Decius, requiring pagan sacrifice; it produced glorious martyrs and many lapsed, raising the question of restoring the fallen.

corruption_summary: The persecution exposed the cost of discipleship and the failure of the unprepared, not a corruption of doctrine but a trial of faith.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the cost of true discipleship and the reality of the world’s enmity against Christ. The Decian Persecution tested the church as fire tests metal: those whose faith was genuine stood firm unto death or endured as confessors, while the unprepared and the false fell away. The Lord had warned that all who would live godly in Christ shall suffer persecution, and bade His own be faithful unto death for the crown of life.

The trial also exposed the danger of an unprepared and nominal Christianity. Many who had professed the faith in easier days sacrificed to idols or bought certificates of compliance when the sword was drawn, showing that not all who bear the name are truly Christ’s. Yet the persecution, by raising the question of the lapsed, also pressed the church to wrestle rightly with repentance and restoration. The dictionary holds the sober lesson: the friendship of the world is not to be expected, the faith must be counted worth dying for, and the church must be ready, in days of peace, for the days of trial that may come.

etymology: Latin lapsi, “the fallen,” from labi, to slip or fall; those who lapsed from the faith under persecution.
biblical_def: The lapsi—Latin for “the fallen”—were those Christians who lapsed from the faith under persecution, especially in the great Decian persecution, by sacrificing to the pagan gods, offering incense, or purchasing certificates that falsely declared they had complied. When the persecution ended, the question of the lapsed became one of the most painful controversies of the early church: on what terms, if any, might those who had denied Christ under threat be received back into communion. Some, the rigorists, held that such apostasy could never be forgiven by the church, or only after lifelong penance. Others, more lax, would restore the fallen too quickly and cheaply, often on the strength of letters from the confessors who had stood firm. The church, chiefly through Cyprian of Carthage, sought a middle and pastoral course: the lapsed were not beyond hope, for Christ receives the penitent, but neither were they to be restored without genuine repentance proved over time, with grades of penance fitted to the gravity of the fall. The dictionary draws from the matter of the lapsi an enduring lesson on apostasy, repentance, and church discipline. Denial of Christ under trial is a grievous sin, yet not unpardonable where there is true repentance, as Peter’s own denial and restoration show; but repentance must be real and not presumed, and the church must guard both the holiness of its communion and the door of mercy for the truly penitent. The case of the fallen teaches that grace is free but not cheap, and that restoration follows repentance, not mere desire to return.
webster_summary: “The fallen”—Christians who lapsed under persecution by sacrificing or buying certificates; their restoration was a painful early-church controversy on apostasy, repentance, and discipline.

corruption_summary: The fallen were met by two errors—a rigorism that denied all hope of restoration and a laxity that restored without true repentance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter of the lapsi exposes two opposite errors the church must avoid in dealing with the fallen. The rigorist error, which hardened into the Novatianist schism, denied that grave post-baptismal sin—apostasy above all—could ever be forgiven by the church, shutting the door of mercy that Christ has opened to the penitent. Peter denied his Lord three times and was restored; the gospel offers pardon to the truly repentant, even for grievous denial.

The opposite error was a cheap laxity that restored the fallen too quickly, on slender evidence and without proof of genuine repentance, treating the holiness of the church’s communion lightly. The dictionary holds the pastoral balance the better early teachers sought: the lapsed are not beyond hope, for grace is free to the penitent; but repentance must be real and proved, not presumed, and restoration follows it rather than mere desire to return. Grace is free but not cheap. The case of the fallen teaches the church to keep both the door of mercy open to the penitent and the purity of its communion guarded against presumption.

etymology: From Greek Pamphilos, “friend of all”; the presbyter and martyr of Caesarea, teacher of Eusebius.
biblical_def: Pamphilus of Caesarea was a presbyter, scholar, and martyr of the late third and early fourth centuries, renowned for his devotion to the Scriptures and for the great library he gathered at Caesarea in Palestine. A man of learning and piety, trained in the tradition of Origen, he devoted himself to copying and correcting the text of the Scriptures and to building a library that became one of the foremost centers of Christian learning in the ancient world, preserving the labors of earlier scholars. His most famous disciple was Eusebius, the church historian, who so honored his teacher that he took the name “Eusebius of Pamphilus” and wrote a biography of him now lost. Pamphilus was imprisoned in the persecution under Maximinus and, after long confinement during which he continued his scholarly labors, was put to death for the faith in 309, winning the martyr’s crown. The dictionary honors Pamphilus as an example of the marriage of scholarship and martyrdom—a man who loved the Scriptures enough both to labor over their text in the library and to die for their Lord in the arena. His devotion to the careful preservation and study of the Word, and his willingness to seal his confession with his blood, make him a worthy witness. The dictionary honors the man and his love of Scripture while remembering that his school stood in the line of Origen, whose speculative theology the later church did not in all things follow; the honor belongs to his fidelity to the Word and his faithfulness unto death.

corruption_summary: The labor of preserving Scripture and the witness of martyrdom are devalued by an age indifferent to both careful learning and costly faith.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the marriage of scholarship and devotion, of careful labor over the Word and willingness to die for its Lord. Pamphilus loved the Scriptures enough both to copy and correct their text in the library and to seal his confession with his blood in the arena. Against an age indifferent to careful learning on one hand and to costly faith on the other, his example joins the diligence of the workman who rightly divides the word of truth with the courage of the martyr faithful unto death.

The dictionary honors the man and his love of Scripture while keeping a discerning eye. Pamphilus stood in the scholarly tradition of Origen, whose speculative theology—on the pre-existence of souls, on the final restoration of all, and other matters—the later church did not in all things follow, and some of which it condemned. The honor due to Pamphilus belongs not to every opinion of his school but to his fidelity to the Word, his labor in preserving it, and his faithfulness unto death. He stands as a witness that the careful study of Scripture and the costly confession of Christ belong together.

etymology: The name of an ancient city of upper Mesopotamia (modern Urfa), an early center of Syriac-speaking Christianity.
biblical_def: Edessa was an ancient city of upper Mesopotamia, in the region between the Roman and Persian empires, which became one of the earliest and most important centers of Syriac-speaking Christianity. According to ancient tradition the gospel reached Edessa very early, and the city embraced Christianity sooner and more thoroughly than most, becoming a stronghold of the faith in the East and a fountainhead of Syriac Christian literature, hymnody, and biblical learning. From Edessa and its school came much of the rich tradition of Syriac Christianity, including the labors that produced the Peshitta, the standard Syriac translation of the Scriptures, and the hymns of Ephrem the Syrian, the greatest of the Syriac fathers. Edessa thus stands as a reminder that the early church was not confined to the Greek and Latin West but spread east into Mesopotamia and beyond, in a language closely akin to the Aramaic that the Lord Jesus Himself spoke. The dictionary notes Edessa as a witness to the early and wide spread of the gospel, fulfilling the commission to be witnesses to the uttermost part of the earth, while remembering that the Syriac churches later became entangled in the Christological controversies, some falling into the Nestorian and others into the Monophysite errors. The honor belongs to the early vigor of the faith there and to its preservation and translation of the Scriptures; the later divisions are a warning of how even ancient and zealous churches may be carried into error when they depart from the orthodox confession of the person of Christ.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the early and wide spread of the gospel, eastward into Mesopotamia and beyond, fulfilling the commission to be witnesses unto the uttermost part of the earth. Edessa is a standing reminder that the church of the first centuries was not confined to the Greek and Latin West, but flourished also in the Syriac-speaking East, in a tongue closely akin to the Aramaic the Lord Himself spoke, producing the Peshitta and the hymns of Ephrem.

Yet Edessa and the Syriac churches are also a warning. In the great Christological controversies of the fifth century, many of the Eastern churches were carried into error—some into the Nestorian division that so separated the natures of Christ as to imperil the unity of His person, others into the Monophysite confusion that so merged them as to lose His true humanity. The dictionary honors the early vigor of the faith at Edessa and its preservation and translation of the Scriptures, while marking that even ancient and zealous churches may be drawn into grievous error when they forsake the orthodox confession of the one Christ in two natures, undivided and unconfused, that Chalcedon rightly maintained.

etymology: From Syriac (the eastern Aramaic dialect of the Syrian church) and Christianity; the tradition of the Aramaic-speaking churches of the East.
biblical_def: Syriac Christianity is the tradition of the Aramaic-speaking churches of the East, who worshipped, wrote, and read the Scriptures in Syriac, a dialect of Aramaic closely akin to the language the Lord Jesus Himself spoke. Centered in upper Mesopotamia, Syria, and stretching eastward through Persia and along the trade routes as far as India and China, Syriac Christianity was a vigorous and distinct branch of the early church, neither Greek nor Latin. It produced the Peshitta, the standard Syriac Bible; a rich tradition of hymnody and poetry, above all in Ephrem the Syrian, who taught theology through song; a vital monastic and missionary movement that carried the gospel deep into Asia centuries before the Western powers; and notable schools of biblical learning. The dictionary notes Syriac Christianity as a witness to the breadth and antiquity of the church and to the early fulfilling of the Great Commission to the uttermost parts of the earth. It honors the missionary zeal, the love of Scripture, and the devotional richness of this tradition, while remembering with sorrow that much of the Syriac East was drawn into the Christological controversies, the Church of the East taking a Nestorian path and the West-Syrian church a Monophysite one. The honor belongs to the genuine faith, learning, and missionary labor of these churches; the divisions are a warning that distance from the great councils and isolation amid hostile empires did not preserve them from error in the doctrine of the person of Christ, which the dictionary holds with Chalcedon.
webster_summary: The tradition of the Aramaic-speaking churches of the East—producers of the Peshitta and Ephrem’s hymns, and great missionaries into Asia—honored for faith and zeal, though much drawn into Christological error.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the breadth and antiquity of the church and the early fulfilling of the Great Commission. Syriac Christianity carried the gospel into Persia, India, and across Asia centuries before the Western powers, producing the Peshitta and the hymns of Ephrem and showing that the sound of the gospel went into all the earth. The dictionary honors the missionary zeal, the love of Scripture, and the devotional richness of this often-forgotten branch of the church.

Yet the Syriac East is also a sober warning. Much of it was drawn into the Christological controversies, the Church of the East following a Nestorian path that so divided the two natures as to imperil the unity of Christ’s person, and the West-Syrian church a Monophysite one that so merged them as to endanger His true humanity. The dictionary holds with Chalcedon the one Christ in two natures, undivided and unconfused, and marks that distance from the great councils and isolation amid hostile empires did not preserve these churches from error in the doctrine of the person of Christ. The honor belongs to their genuine faith and labor; the divisions teach that zeal without orthodoxy is not enough.

etymology: From Syrian (of the Syriac church) and typology (the interpretation of Old Testament types fulfilled in Christ); the rich symbolic and typological reading of Scripture in the Syriac tradition.
biblical_def: Syrian typology refers to the rich symbolic and typological manner of reading and teaching the Scriptures that marked the Syriac Christian tradition, above all in the hymns and writings of Ephrem the Syrian. Where the Greek and Latin fathers often expounded the faith through formal philosophical and doctrinal argument, the Syriac tradition characteristically taught through symbol, type, and poetic image—tracing the figures and shadows of the Old Testament to their fulfillment in Christ, and finding the whole creation full of pointers to the Creator and Redeemer. Ephrem in particular saw types and symbols everywhere: the wood of the ark and the tree of life pointing to the cross, the Passover lamb to the Lamb of God, the manna to the bread of life, Eden to paradise restored. This typological reading, at its best, is deeply biblical, for the Scriptures themselves teach that the Old Testament persons, events, and institutions were types and shadows of good things to come, fulfilled in Christ, and the New Testament reads them so. The dictionary commends genuine, Scripture-governed typology as a faithful way of reading the Bible as one book with Christ at its center, and honors the Syriac tradition’s love of finding Christ in all the Scriptures. It marks, however, that typology must be governed by the text and by the New Testament’s own use, lest it run loose into fanciful allegory that finds in Scripture whatever the interpreter pleases. True typology, the dictionary holds, is the disciplined discernment of the types God Himself appointed and the apostles confirmed, not the unbounded invention of hidden meanings.
webster_summary: The rich symbolic, typological reading of Scripture in the Syriac tradition, above all in Ephrem—tracing Old Testament types to Christ; commended where Scripture-governed, guarded against fanciful allegory.

corruption_summary: Typology, when ungoverned by the text, degenerates into fanciful allegory that finds in Scripture whatever the interpreter pleases.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is genuine, Scripture-governed typology—the reading of the Bible as one book with Christ at its center, in which the persons, events, and institutions of the Old Testament were types and shadows of good things to come, fulfilled in Him. The Syriac tradition’s love of finding Christ in all the Scriptures, taught through symbol and song, is at its best deeply biblical, for the Scriptures themselves so read the law as a shadow of good things to come, and the risen Lord expounded Moses and the prophets concerning Himself.

The danger, which the dictionary marks, is the slide from disciplined typology into fanciful allegory—the unbounded invention of hidden meanings that finds in every detail of the text whatever the interpreter pleases, untethered from the author’s intent and the New Testament’s own use. The remedy is not to abandon typology, which Scripture itself employs, but to govern it: true typology discerns the types God Himself appointed and the apostles confirmed, reading the Old Testament through the New, rather than spinning allegories of its own. So governed, the typological reading is a faithful and fruitful way of beholding Christ in all the Scriptures.

etymology: From Greek pneuma (spirit) and machomai (to fight); “fighters against the Spirit,” the fourth-century deniers of the deity of the Holy Spirit.
biblical_def: The Pneumatomachians—Greek for “fighters against the Spirit”—were a fourth-century party that denied the full deity of the Holy Spirit, holding Him to be a creature or a ministering power rather than true God, the third Person of the Trinity. Having largely accepted, after Nicaea, the deity of the Son, they balked at extending the same confession to the Spirit, and so were also called Macedonians after Macedonius, a bishop associated with the error. Against them the church confessed the full deity of the Holy Spirit, drawing from the Scriptures that call the Spirit God, ascribe to Him the divine attributes and works, and join Him with the Father and the Son in the one name into which believers are baptized. The great defenders of orthodoxy in this controversy were the Cappadocian fathers—Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa—and the matter was settled at the Council of Constantinople in 381, which expanded the Nicene Creed to confess the Holy Spirit as “the Lord, the Giver of life, who proceedeth from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified.” The dictionary names the Pneumatomachian error as a denial of the Trinity no less serious than Arianism, for to deny the deity of the Spirit is to deny the triune God and to leave the church without a divine Sanctifier. Scripture is plain: to lie to the Holy Ghost is to lie to God; the Spirit searches the deep things of God; and the believer is the temple of the Spirit who dwells within. The dictionary confesses with the church the full and equal deity of the Holy Spirit, true God with the Father and the Son.
webster_summary: The fourth-century “fighters against the Spirit” (Macedonians) who denied the deity of the Holy Spirit; answered by the Cappadocians and condemned at Constantinople in 381.

corruption_summary: The Pneumatomachians denied the deity of the Holy Spirit, dismembering the Trinity by refusing the Spirit the worship due to God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the denial of the full deity of the Holy Spirit—the reduction of the third Person of the Trinity to a creature or an impersonal power. This is a denial of the triune God no less serious than the Arian denial of the Son, for the one God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and to subtract the Spirit’s deity is to dismember the Godhead and leave the church without a divine Sanctifier. Scripture forbids it: to lie to the Holy Ghost is to lie to God; the Spirit searches the deep things of God; the three are named together in the one baptismal name.

The dictionary confesses with the church catholic the full and equal deity of the Holy Spirit, true God with the Father and the Son, worshipped and glorified together with Them. The Cappadocian fathers defended this truth, and the Council of Constantinople in 381 enshrined it in the expanded Nicene Creed: the Holy Spirit is “the Lord, the Giver of life, who proceedeth from the Father, who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified.” The Pneumatomachian error, though it sounds remote, is renewed wherever the Spirit is treated as a mere force or influence rather than the divine Person He is; the dictionary holds the orthodox confession of the Trinity entire.

etymology: From Novatian, the third-century Roman presbyter who led the schism; a rigorist movement over the readmission of the lapsed.
biblical_def: Novatianism was a third-century rigorist schism led by Novatian, a learned presbyter of Rome, over the question of the readmission of those who had lapsed under the Decian persecution. Novatian held that the church had no power to grant forgiveness and restoration to those who had committed apostasy after baptism, and that such grievous sinners must be left to the mercy of God without being received back into communion. When a more lenient bishop was elected at Rome, Novatian set himself up as a rival bishop and formed a separate, purist church, calling his followers katharoi, “the pure.” The movement spread and persisted for centuries, marked by its rigorist refusal to readmit the lapsed and, in some forms, by a general severity toward post-baptismal sin. The dictionary judges Novatianism a serious error, however earnest its zeal for the holiness of the church. It rightly prized purity but wrongly denied the gospel of repentance and the church’s authority to receive the penitent. Scripture holds out forgiveness to the truly repentant, even for grievous sins: Peter denied his Lord and was restored; if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive. To shut the door of restoration against the penitent is to deny the very gospel of grace and to make the church purer than her Lord, who came to call sinners to repentance and receives all who come. The dictionary holds the balance the great teachers sought: the church must guard its holiness by requiring real repentance, yet must keep open the door of mercy that Christ has opened to every penitent sinner.
webster_summary: A third-century rigorist schism under Novatian, denying the church’s power to restore the lapsed; it prized purity but wrongly shut the door of repentance against the penitent.
webster_full: NOVATIANISM, a third-century rigorist schism under the Roman presbyter Novatian.

corruption_summary: Novatianism shut the door of restoration against penitent sinners, denying the gospel of repentance in the name of purity.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the rigorist denial of restoration to the penitent—the teaching that the church has no power to forgive and readmit those who lapsed into apostasy after baptism. Zealous for purity, Novatianism shut the door of mercy that Christ has opened, leaving grievous sinners without hope of return however truly they repented. Scripture holds out forgiveness to the penitent: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive; heaven rejoices over one sinner that repents; Paul bids the church forgive and comfort the restored.

The dictionary honors the Novatianist concern for the holiness of the church while rejecting its error. The church must indeed guard its purity and require real repentance, not cheap or presumed; but to deny restoration to the truly penitent is to make the church holier than her Lord and to deny the gospel of grace. Peter denied Christ and was restored to feed the sheep. The remedy for laxity is not rigorism but the right balance: a door of mercy kept open to every penitent sinner, and a discipline that requires repentance to be real. Novatianism, by erring on the side of severity, became a schism and a denial of the very grace it claimed to honor.
roots_summary: The movement’s name marks the rigorist schism that, prizing purity, denied the penitent the gospel of restoration.
